358.title: Jaap for courage
358.hook: many Sikhs turn to Jaap when they need strength
358.howItsDone: Some Sikhs recite or listen to Jaap Sahib when they need strength, before exams, surgery, journeys or hard conversations, as well as in their daily Nitnem.

segments.voice: Yesterday, amrit, the water Jaap is recited into, and your line, prayer stirred in. Today, what Jaap is for on a hard day.

The waiting room before the scan. The car outside the job interview. The hallway before the hard conversation with your father. The heart is going too fast, and every bit of advice, just breathe, you've got this, sounds thin. What people actually do in that moment is reach for something: a song with a beat, a friend's voice on the phone, a line they know by heart. Ask some Sikhs what they reach for, and you may hear the same answer.
screen: `THE WAITING ROOM BEFORE THE SCAN.` → `ADVICE SOUNDS THIN.` → `WHAT DO YOU REACH FOR?`

segments.voice: Some Sikhs say that when they need strength, they turn to Jaap Sahib: before an exam, before surgery, on a long night drive, at a hospital bedside. Some recite it under their breath; some play a recording in the car. Why Jaap, of all the banis? Three reasons are often given. First, the words. Jaap is full of what a frightened person needs to hear: ajai, unconquerable; abhai, fearless; alai, indestructible; the protector with weapons in hand; the One who holds even death. Said aloud, they push back against the weight. Second, the rhythm. You heard it at the drums three days ago: the quick meters make your breath fall into time, and a steadier breath makes the next step easier. Third, the voice. Jaap is the Tenth Guru's. Sikhs know his story: a father executed, a city lost, four sons lost, and Sikh tradition remembers him in chardi kala, rising spirits, through all of it. Reciting Jaap, a Sikh isn't trying to manufacture courage from nothing. They're borrowing it, from a Guru who had every reason to be afraid and who, as Sikhs remember him, kept going. And Jaap never says the hard thing won't happen. It doesn't promise a good scan or a passed exam. Sikhs hear it reminding the one reciting who stands with them while it happens. That's the courage on offer: not certainty about the outcome, but company in it.

segments.voice: Think of one hard thing coming up; if you can, play a minute of Jaap Sahib now and let its rhythm steady your breath, and if you can't, say a few lines you know: ajai, alai, abhai, abai. Then picture yourself walking into that hard moment, not alone, with the rhythm still going inside you, and breathe slowly.
Bal, strength. Some Sikhs turn to Jaap when they need it, borrowing the Tenth Guru's fearlessness in his own words and rhythm.
Your line: borrow the courage. Not certainty about the outcome, but company in it. Day three hundred fifty-eight.

359.title: Why so many names
359.hook: a thousand names say that no single name can hold Him
359.howItsDone: Sikhs call the One by many names in prayer and kirtan, Waheguru, Akal Purakh, Ram, Hari, Gobind, Kartar and more, following the Guru Granth Sahib, which uses names from many languages.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bal, strength, and your line, borrow the courage. Today, a step back to look at the whole hymn and ask a simple question.

How many names do you have? Your full name on forms. A shorter one for friends. Something only your grandmother called you. Mom, or Dad, or Auntie, to someone. A nickname from a soccer team you'd rather forget. Each one is true, each holds a different piece of you, and not one of them is the whole person. So what happens when the one being named is infinitely larger than any person?
screen: `A NAME ON FORMS, A NAME FOR FRIENDS.` → `WHAT YOUR GRANDMOTHER CALLED YOU.` → `NO ONE NAME IS THE WHOLE PERSON.`

segments.voice: Over the last four weeks you've heard a tiny slice of Jaap's names. Timeless. Merciful. Formless. Unborn. The armed One. Sun of suns. Lamp of beauty. Provider. Gobind. Home of compassion. Fearless. Hundreds more are still waiting. Why so many? Jaap answered in its first stanza: who can tell all Your names? The wise speak the names drawn from Your deeds. So the long list isn't trying to finish the job. It admits the job can't be finished, and praises anyway. Each name is a window into one room of a house too big to see at once. Guru Nanak said the same in the nineteenth pauri of Japji: countless are Your names, countless Your places. Then he adds that even the word countless is too heavy to carry. Notice where the names come from, too. The Guru Granth Sahib calls the One by names from many places: Ram, Hari and Gobind, which Hindus also use; Allah, Khuda and Rahim, which Muslims also use; and Waheguru, the name that became the Sikh word of wonder. Jaap adds Sanskrit, Persian and Arabic names of its own. Sikhs don't treat any one of these as the password. The One, Sikh teaching holds, is beyond them all, and present in each. It's like the stars: the more you look, the more there are.
screen: `HUNDREDS OF NAMES IN ONE HYMN.` · `NO LIST CAN FINISH THE JOB.` · `JAPJI 19: COUNTLESS ARE YOUR NAMES.` · `NAMES FROM MANY LANGUAGES.` · then, large: `MORE NAMES THAN STARS.`

segments.voice: Write three names for the Divine: ones you've learned here, like Akal or Kripaal, ones from your own background, or deed-names from your own life, like the one who carried me last winter. If the word Divine doesn't fit you, write three names for whatever you feel grateful toward. Read them slowly, and notice that each one opens a different window.
Asankh naav, countless names. No single name can hold the One: Jaap's hundreds of names admit the list can never be finished, and praise anyway.
Your line: more names than stars. Nobody has ever counted either of them. See you tomorrow.

360.title: The whole Jaap
360.hook: all 199 stanzas take about fifteen to twenty minutes
360.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite the whole of Jaap Sahib every morning, from memory or a gutka, in about fifteen to twenty minutes, and many others listen to recordings while traveling or getting ready for the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, asankh naav, countless names, and your line, more names than stars. Today, all of them at once: the whole hymn, start to finish.

You've seen a cathedral, a gurdwara or a mountain in pieces. A photo of a doorway, a close-up of a carving, one window, one dome. Then one day you stand across the valley, see the whole thing at once, and every piece makes sense where it sits. For four weeks you've looked at Jaap Sahib one window at a time. Today you step back across the valley.
screen: `A BUILDING SEEN IN PIECES.` → `THEN, ACROSS THE VALLEY, ALL OF IT.` → `EVERY PIECE MAKES SENSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the map. Recited at a steady pace, all one hundred ninety-nine stanzas take about fifteen to twenty minutes. It opens with one big stanza, the chhappai, that clears the table: no mark, no caste, no lineage; king of kings; named by deeds. Then the snake begins to glide, bhujang prayat: namastvam akaale, namastvam kripaale, salutation after salutation. The meter shortens to the quick two-word steps of chachari: aroop hain, anoop hain, ajoo hain, abhoo hain. Further along, the language turns to Persian and Arabic: the lamp of beauty, the giver of daily bread. Longer rolling lines, roaal, bring one form, many sights. The tiny harbolmana lines give the home of compassion and the breaker of the cruel. The one-letter meter flies: ajai, alai, abhai, abai. Between them, other meters you haven't met yet, each with its own walk. And the end returns to the glide, gathering everything into sadaa sachidaanand, and the last words, ever by your side. Seen whole, the shape is clear. It begins by saying what the One isn't, spends nearly two hundred stanzas on what the One does and is, in rhythm after rhythm and more than one language, and ends by saying the One is right here. That's why many Sikhs say Jaap is best known not in pieces but said whole, every morning, until it lives in the body. The words you've learned, akaal, kripaal, aroop, abhai, are signposts along that road.

361.title: Jaap close
361.hook: the Tenth Guru's praise now sits beside Nanak's Japji in your morning
361.howItsDone: In the Sikh morning Nitnem, Japji Sahib is recited first and Jaap Sahib second, followed by the Tav Prasad Savaiye; many Sikhs say all three before or around dawn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, naam, and your line, all the names: the whole hymn, start to finish. Today, the last of our thirty days with Jaap Sahib.

Some mornings have a shape you'd recognize in the dark. Feet on the cold floor. Water on the face. The kettle, the same mug. In Sikh homes that keep Nitnem, the shape has words too, in a fixed order. First a quiet, thoughtful voice, the first Guru's. Then a faster one, written generations later, with a drumbeat in it. Thirty days ago you only knew the first.
screen: `A MORNING YOU'D KNOW IN THE DARK.` → `FIRST A QUIET VOICE.` → `THEN A FASTER ONE WITH A DRUMBEAT.`

segments.voice: Put the two side by side. Japji is Guru Nanak's, the first Guru, and it opens the Guru Granth Sahib on page one. Jaap is Guru Gobind Singh's, the tenth Guru, and it opens the Dasam Granth. Two first pages, two Gurus many generations apart. Japji begins with Ik Onkar, One, and the Mool Mantar: true Name, creator, without fear, without hatred, timeless, unborn. Jaap begins with no mark, no caste, then salutes the One as akaal, abhai, ajooni. Same truths, different walk. Japji thinks its way forward, pauri by pauri, asking questions. Jaap marches, name after name, through many meters and languages. Sikhs believe the same light, the same jot, passed from Guru Nanak to each Guru in turn. Saying Japji and then Jaap each morning is a small way of hearing that: the first Guru's voice, then the tenth, and the light in both. Now look back at the road. The morning praise, Jaap Sahib. No mark, no caste. King of kings. Named by deeds. The snake's gait. Akaal, the Timeless. The Merciful. Formless, beyond compare. Ajooni, unborn. The armed One, the protector. Sun of suns. Song of songs. The lamp of beauty. The provider. Gobind. One form, many sights. Ender and sustainer. Karunaa, the house of compassion. Breaker of the cruel. The one-letter meter. Abhai. Every land. Beyond the fear of death. Keeping the pace. The last stanza. The amrit bowl. Courage. So many names. The whole Jaap. Tomorrow, the third morning bani: ten verses under the heading by your grace.

362.title: By your grace
362.hook: the heading means by Your grace; ten verses follow
362.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite the ten Tav Prasad Savaiye each morning after Jaap Sahib, and they are among the five banis read while amrit is prepared at the Khalsa initiation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nitnem, the daily round, and your line, japji, then jaap. Today, the third morning bani begins.

Stand in line at a gurdwara near the end of the service and watch people's hands. A sevadar comes down the row with a bowl of warm karah prasad, the sweet made of flour, ghee and sugar. Nobody reaches in and takes a scoop. Each person holds out two cupped hands, and a spoonful is placed in them. Even a toddler learns it: hands together, open, waiting. You don't earn it at the counter. You receive it. The next bani of the Sikh morning has that same word written over its door.
screen: `A BOWL OF WARM KARAH PRASAD.` → `TWO HANDS, CUPPED AND OPEN.` → `RECEIVED, NOT TAKEN.`

segments.voice: Tav prasad. Tav means your; prasad means grace, a gift freely given. It's the same prasad as the sweet in your hands, and the same word that closes the Mool Mantar: gur prasad, by the Guru's grace. Guru Gobind Singh writes tav prasad as a heading again and again, over section after section, like a dedication at the top of every page. Here it heads ten short poems, the Tav Prasad Savaiye. A savaiya is a verse form of four long, swinging lines, made for reciting aloud. These ten come from the Tenth Guru's Akal Ustat, the praise of the Timeless One, written in Braj, a literary language of north India in his day. Sikhs who keep Nitnem say them every morning, right after the Jaap, and they're among the five banis recited while the amrit is prepared at the Khalsa initiation. Here's the surprise. After a heading like by your grace, you'd expect soft, comforting verses. Instead the ten savaiye march past everything people in the Guru's world admired: ascetics and yogis, elephants hung with gold, emperors with beating drums, pilgrims at every river, rituals of every kind. After each parade, the verses set it all down and say, in effect, that without the Lord's love and grace it weighs nothing. So the heading is the key. Everything below it is what people try to achieve; the heading names what can only be received. Over the next week, the parade, one float at a time.

segments.voice: Rest your hands in your lap, palms up and a little cupped, the way people hold them for karah prasad. Notice three things you're holding right now that you didn't make: the breath going in, the light in the room, the fact that you woke up today. If you pray, whisper Waheguru as each one lands.

363.title: The ascetics I have seen
363.hook: the poet has seen hosts of monks, siddhas and yogis, yet without love for the Lord it is all worth nothing (Savaiye 1)
363.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this savaiya each morning as the first of the ten Tav Prasad Savaiye, and it is often explained in the gurdwara as a warning against outward religion without love.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tav prasad, by your grace, and your line, cupped hands, waiting. Now the first of the ten verses.

A traveler has made it his business to see every holy person in the land. He's sat outside the huts of ascetics who've given up everything. He's watched yogis hold impossible postures for hours. He's met celibates, wonder-workers, wandering monks, holy men of every order. Some could do things you and I can't. At the end of all that traveling, he sits down to write what he's learned, and it comes out in one breath.
screen: `A TRAVELER WHO HAS SEEN THEM ALL.` → `ASCETICS, YOGIS, MONKS.` → `WHAT DID HE LEARN?`

segments.voice: That traveler is the voice of the first savaiya. In paraphrase: I have wandered and seen hosts of pure ascetics, siddhas, the dwellings of yogis and celibates. I have seen heroes and gods and sages, the holy men of sect after sect, the religious ways of every country. Then the last line turns: without the love and grace of the Lord, all of this isn't worth one ratti. A ratti is a tiny red seed, used as a small weight for gold. So the verse puts the whole parade of holiness on a jeweler's scale, and without love the pan doesn't tip. This is easy to hear wrong. It isn't sneering at discipline; the poet went out to see these people. Sikh teaching favors the householder's life over the cave, but this verse doesn't sneer at those who chose the cave. Its point is narrower and harder. A person can sit for years, give up food, give up sleep, and if love isn't at the center, the verse says it's weightless. And it isn't only about other people's practices. Sikhs often hear it as a mirror: early rising, long recitations, a person's own discipline can go on the same scale. Said in the morning, before the day's practice begins, the verse asks what's at the center. Its answer is one word. Love.

364.title: Elephants in gold
364.hook: drunken elephants decked in gold, horses swift as deer, kings in glory, and all leave this world empty-handed (Savaiye 2)
364.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this as the second of the ten Tav Prasad Savaiye each morning; it is often explained as a reminder that wealth and power stay behind when a person dies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prem, and your line, nothing without love. This week: courage borrowed, more names than stars, all the names, japji then jaap, cupped hands waiting, and nothing without love. Today, the second verse.

The parade comes down the road and the crowd goes quiet. First the elephants, huge and swaying, drunk on their own strength, hung with gold that flashes in the sun. Then the horses, thousands of them, quick as deer, barely touching the ground. Then the kings, broad in the shoulder, with rows of people bowing their heads on either side. Nobody can look away. And the poet leans over and whispers one question.
screen: `ELEPHANTS FLASHING WITH GOLD.` → `HORSES QUICK AS DEER.` → `KINGS, AND ROWS OF BOWED HEADS.`

segments.voice: That's the second savaiya. In paraphrase: maddened elephants decked in gold, tall and matchless. Horses by the million, leaping like deer, outrunning the wind. Mighty kings before whom countless heads bow. Then the question: and what of it? Such great kings there have been, and at the end they went away barefoot. In the Guru's world, a king never walked anywhere. He rode. So the one who arrived on an elephant leaves on his own bare feet, carrying nothing, empty-handed, the way everyone leaves. What keeps this from easy moralizing is the man writing it. Guru Gobind Singh knew this world from the inside. He held court at Anandpur. He rode fine horses, and Sikh tradition tells of an elephant called Prasadi, brought to the young Guru as a gift. He'd seen the gold up close and knew what it could and couldn't do. Notice what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't call elephants evil or beautiful things wrong; Sikhs aren't asked to give up their homes or their work. It simply follows the parade to its end, past the city gates, to the last walk every king takes, where the gold stays behind. It doesn't say here what should be carried instead. It leaves the question standing at the gate: if not the gold, then what?

segments.voice: Pick up one thing you own, a watch, a mug, a ring, and really look at it: where it came from, what it's been through with you. Enjoy it honestly, without guilt, and let a second, light thought sit beside the first: one day it won't be yours. Smile at it the way you'd smile at a friend you know you'll part from one day.
